title: Nationwide unveils 1% deposit mortgage deal for first-time buyers
author: Rupert Jones
text:
People can borrow up to six times their income, but brokers sound alarm over risks of negative equity if house prices fall

A mortgage deal that lets first-time buyers borrow 99% of a property’s value has prompted warnings that even a small dip in house prices could result in borrowers falling into negative equity.

On Wednesday, Nationwide unveiled a mortgage enabling people to buy a home with just a 1% deposit and potentially borrow up to six times their income.

Britain’s biggest building society said it was putting £1bn a year behind the new product, which it believes will open up home ownership to more than 5,000 additional first-time buyers each year.

During the last couple of years, a number of mortgages have gone on sale that require only a small deposit, or no deposit at all. Nationwide said its 99% home loan would “combine meaningful support with responsible lending” – but the mortgage’s launch coincided with data suggesting UK house prices were falling amid the continuing challenging economic conditions.

Lloyds bank said UK house prices dropped by 0.6% in October and were down 1.2% year on year, while the property firm Savills said this month that average prices were expected to drift lower during the rest of 2026 and fall by 1.5% in 2027 .

The Nationwide product is a five-year fixed-rate deal with an interest rate of 5.99%. While many commentators have welcomed it as a lifeline to struggling first-time buyers, some brokers cautioned borrowers could be pushed into negative equity if prices did fall. Negative equity is when someone is living in a property worth less than their mortgage.

Negative equity can leave homeowners trapped, unable to climb the housing ladder as their homes reduce in value.

Riz Malik, an independent financial adviser at the firm R3 Wealth, said: “Nationwide is sticking its neck out with a 1% deposit deal, as even a small slip in prices could leave borrowers in negative equity.”

Darryl Dhoffer, the founder of the brokerage firm The Mortgage Geezer, said those signing up “must tread carefully”. He added: “Borrowing up to six times income at a 5.99% rate creates massive monthly commitments and leaves almost zero equity buffer – meaning even a slight market dip could trigger negative equity.”

Negative equity mainly becomes a problem when homeowners intend to sell their property. As a result, the Nationwide deal was probably most suitable for those buyers “planning to stay put well beyond five years”, said Craig Fish, the managing director of the broker Lodestone Mortgages .

He added: “This is a genuine step forward for first-time buyers who can afford the monthly payments but can’t save a deposit while paying rent.”

Henry Jordan, Nationwide’s group director of mortgages, said “a range of controls” were built into the product to reduce the risk of negative equity.

The deal is only available as a five-year fix, providing certainty over monthly payments, and is restricted to “used” houses only meaning it will not be available to those buying a flat or a newbuild home.

In addition, every applicant must receive mortgage advice and “robust” affordability checks will be carried out, with minimum income requirements imposed and the exclusion of self-employed people.

Jordan added: “I don’t think anyone is forecasting a fall in house prices over the next five years.”

Savills said it expected UK house prices to rise by 15.8% – or £56,500 on average – over the five years to 2031, adding that price growth was expected to accelerate during the second half of 2028.

title: High prices force many across the US to scale back for Thanksgiving: ‘We can’t afford the food’
author: Anna Betts
text:
Americans are opting for smaller gatherings, reconsidering travel or swapping expensive ingredients for cheaper alternatives

Thanksgiving is just one day away, but for some Americans, the holiday may look a little different this year as higher costs for food, drinks , household goods, air travel and gasoline have prompted some families to rethink their plans and spending.

The Guardian recently asked readers across the United States how they were marking the holiday this year and whether higher prices had affected their plans or made them rethink their usual traditions.

While some said their plans remained unchanged, many said that they were scaling back and cutting costs. Some said that they were opting for smaller gatherings, reconsidering travel or choosing not to host at all. Others said they were swapping more expensive ingredients for cheaper alternatives or cooking less than they normally would.

In Florida, one man in his 60s said that he and his girlfriend were “scaling way back” this year.

“The expense has made it impossible for us to have what we usually do,” he said, adding that “food is horribly expensive”.

Instead of doing three different pies, they are preparing just one this year, along with a single side dish.

Cindy Van Vreede, 66, in Wisconsin, told the Guardian that the senior center where she goes for “free meals several times a week, is offering to bring a free Thanksgiving dinner to me at my home”.

“By not traveling or expected to bring a dish, I am saving money staying at home,” she said. “I’m also saving money on gas because I’m not driving my car two hours each way.”

A recent report from the American Farm Bureau Federation estimated that Americans preparing a Thanksgiving meal will face “higher prices overall this year”, with the average cost of a 10-person dinner up 6% from last year. It marks the first time since 2022 that American shoppers will see an increase “in the price of goods for Thanksgiving dinner”, according to the report.

The increase for this year is “largely driven by increased prices for Thanksgiving staples such as turkey, milk, rolls and cranberries”, the report says, noting the increases “aren’t a complete surprise as the effects of significant spikes in prices for critical inputs throughout the supply chain, like fuel for processing and transportation, have made their way to consumers”.

America’s farmers and ranchers, the report states, are also facing “significant challenges, with record diesel costs, elevated fertilizer prices, increased labor expenses, and a bigger bill for items like rent and electricity – all of which hurt their ability to break even at the end of the year”.

In Texas, 55-year-old Cheryl said that she was “probably not going to celebrate this year”.

“I’ll miss it, just getting together with my family,” she said, “but we can’t afford the food, and going to a friend’s house is unlikely, too.”

Cheryl said that she had watched as her “regular weekly groceries have gone up so much it’s getting harder to afford them”.

Others are finding ways to preserve some of their traditions while spending less.

In Virginia, 39-year-old Hannah told the Guardian: “We’re going low-key.”

“This year, I’m sticking with a few essential dishes – turkey, gravy, potatoes, cranberries, and mac and cheese,” she said. “I’m using recipes that use cheaper ingredients. I’m having my 10-year-old make Kraft mac and cheese from the box rather than using a homemade recipe with more expensive cheeses.”

Hannah said that she was spending “more time than ever looking at prices at different stores, and I’ve been using store loyalty programs to squeeze extra savings”.

A recent survey by Lending Tree found that, among those planning to celebrate Thanksgiving, more than half said that inflation was affecting their plans or budget, with 25% saying that they were changing their food choices as a result, 22% saying they were using more coupons and 14% saying they were cutting back on guests.

The survey also found that nearly two-thirds of respondents said that they may need to borrow to host Thanksgiving, including 38% who said they planned to use credit cards to cover the costs.

In Seattle, Liliya said that she was trying to persuade her partner “not to order the whole turkey but to buy a few cuts instead”.

Their Thanksgiving, she said, “will be a very small family gathering, no different from other years outside of me trying to scale down on the turkey”.

For others, the expense of traveling for the holiday has prompted a change of plans. A woman in North Carolina said that she had decided not to travel this year, partly due to the cost of “fuel and lodging”.

Instead, she said, they will be treating themselves to a restaurant meal.

title: A familiar Iranian hacking group has found a new way to cause chaos
author: Tom Wilson, Financial Times
text:
Hackers have targeted commercial fridges and freezers before, but never at this scale and never in the heart of Europe. The brazen attack left cyber professionals unsure as to who might have executed such a madcap operation. But French intelligence agencies found traces of Farsi and other clues in the digital trail pointing to an elite hacking unit of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.

The unit allegedly behind the hack, Shahid Kaveh, was already well known to Western intelligence agencies. Named after Mahmoud Kaveh, an Iranian commander who died during the 1980s Iran-Iraq war, it is one of several hacking units overseen by the Revolutionary Guards’ Cyber Electronic Command.

title: China sends first foreign astronaut to ISS rival as it globalises space operations
author: Rebecca Bailey and agencies
text:
Muhammad Zeeshan Ali – the first Pakistani to reach orbit – greeted with Chinese ‘space handshake’ at Tiangong station

China has flown the first foreign astronaut to its Tiangong space station, starting what it says will be the globalisation of its space operations as the US-led International Space Station (ISS) enters its final years of operation.

Floating through a hatch to enter Tiangong, Pakistan’s Muhammad Zeeshan Ali grinned broadly as he was embraced by the onboard crew in what China’s space agency called the country’s first foreign “space handshake”.

Tiangong, completed in 2022, is the jewel in the crown of China’s space programme. The government has invested billions into its celestial ambitions in recent years to catch up with the US and Russia, two of the five partners involved in the ISS, along with Europe, Japan and Canada. After 25 years of continuous occupation, the ISS is set to cease operations from 2030, according to Nasa.

On Wednesday China’s president, Xi Jinping, told his Pakistani counterpart Beijing was “willing to work with all countries … to uphold the banner of the peaceful use of outer space”.

Ali was part of the crew of Shenzhou 24, the most recent iteration of the series of missions that rotate astronauts in the space station every six months. He is the first Pakistani to reach orbit.

“Sending another country’s astronaut to space is a major undertaking,” Blaine Curcio, the managing director at Orbital Gateway Consulting, told the Guardian. “Pakistan is putting a lot of trust into Beijing by having him fly into space on a Chinese-built rocket. There are also considerations related to security: Ali is getting detailed insights into China’s crewed space programme … It makes China better prepared to do it again, and also makes it clear to other countries that China is open to this type of collaboration.”

Space cooperation between China and Pakistan dates back to the early 1990s. China has launched Pakistani satellites and a Pakistani-built rover ‌is also due to fly on a Chinese lunar mission around 2028.

Shenzhou 24 blasted off from the Jiuquan launch centre in north-west China against a pink-tinged dawn sky on Wednesday, footage showed, and first docked with the space station three and a half hours later.

Ali, a 40-year-old Pakistan air force pilot and payload specialist, will conduct experiments including one cultivating microalgae as a potential food and another testing the effects of spaceflight on quinoa seeds. To prepare for the mission, he ​trained for seven months in Beijing, including intensive Chinese-language classes.

At a press conference the day before the launch, Ali recited a line from a classical Chinese poem. Commander Tang Hongbo told reporters that differences in language and culture had made learning to work together more challenging, but that the effort had paid off.

Ali will not stay for the six-month term usually demanded of Tiangong astronauts. Instead, he will return to earth with two of the Shenzhou 23 crew while its commander, Zhu Yangzhu, will remain to complete another milestone – the first full-year stay in space by a Chinese astronout.

Beijing’s accelerated achievements in the skies have spooked its rivals. China is the third country to put humans in orbit and has landed robotic rovers on Mars and the moon, where it hopes to send crewed missions within the next decade. In racing to the moon before 2030, Beijing is competing with the US’s Artemis programme . The US has excluded China from the ISS since 2011, banning Nasa from collaborating with Beijing. In 2025 Nasa went further by blocking Chinese citizens from its facilities altogether.

“We know that China is quite keen to develop Tiangong as an international hub,” said Curcio, pointing to China Manned Space Agency documents published in coordination with the UN outlining “resources for international cooperation” onboard the station.

In the future, he said, he would expect countries such as Brazil and Egypt to seek out the opportunity to send astronauts on Chinese missions. He added: “I think when the ISS is retired, if there is no western replacement (government or commercial), then yes, we may eventually see European or other ISS-involved countries – like Russia – send astronauts to Tiangong.”

title: Swiss tourist killed and British and Americans injured by elephants in Cameroon
author: Rachel Savage in Johannesburg
text:
Alain Throo, insurance executive based in London, reportedly gored and later died on hike near Mount Cameroon national park

A Swiss tourist has been killed and British and American tourists have been injured when a group of hikers encountered a herd of elephants in Cameroon .

The group of six tourists, four British, one Swiss and one American, accompanied by local guides, were hiking near the village of Bakingili in the south of the Mount Cameroon national park on 19 November, on a path used by elephants to access a nearby lake, when they encountered the herd of about 15 animals, according to media reports.

The elephants attacked the group and Alain Throo, a Swiss insurance executive based in London, was reportedly gored and one of the guides tossed into a ditch on top of Throo, while the others hid in trees.

Throo had a black eye and was initially responsive and complaining about an injury to his arm, one of the British female hikers told Cameroonian media, which said they had feared he was bleeding internally.

“He said that the elephant attacked him,” an unidentified Cameroonian man added, according to a video posted by CBS Radio Buea FM. “It smashed him.”

Throo later died of his injuries and his body was carried out of the park by a combined team of park staff and the military to a mortuary in the town of Limbeon 21 November. The American hiker was treated at the same hospital and later discharged, according to local media .

One of the British tourists, who said he had hid in a tree stump for two hours, recalled the moment the elephants attacked their group. “I saw these elephants almost next to me. And I thought, if I go down this path as well, I’m going to get hit. So I just moved to the opposite direction. They ran down the path, I ran and hid in a bush. And I heard some screaming.”

Sean McGovern, the UK chief executive of the insurer Axa XL, where Throo had worked for 13 years, confirmed the death, saying Throo was a “valued member of our team, respected colleague and friend whose contribution, professionalism and warmth touched many people”.

Cameroonian media reported that clashes between elephants and local people had been happening for the past 10 years.

Mount Cameroon is the highest mountain in west and central Africa, at more than 4,000 metres. The African forest elephant was declared critically endangered by the International Union for Conservation of Nature in 2021. There are about 195,000 left in the wild, less than 15% of its population 50 years ago, according to the World Wildlife Fund .

Just 5% of forest elephants, which are smaller than their savannah-based counterparts, are found outside central Africa. In Cameroon, there are about 6,000 forest elephants, according to the NGO Global Conservation , which said the species was at risk from poaching syndicates.

A spokesperson for Britain’s Foreign Office said: “We offered assistance after a number of British nationals were injured in Cameroon.”

title: Nike is Coming Back to Pro Cycling
author: Jim Cotton
text:
The iconic Nike Swoosh will return to the pro peloton in 2027.

Team Visma-Lease a Bike revealed Wednesday that Nike will collaborate with its current kit supplier Nimbl in an R&D arrangement that hints there’s more to come from the U.S. superbrand.

Starting next year, superstar riders like Jonas Vingegaard, Pauline Ferrand-Prévot, and Sepp Kuss will wear kits manufactured by Nimbl but featuring both Nike and Nimbl’s logos.

A Visma-Lease a Bike statement Wednesday suggested all parties will benefit from what could be a landmark moment for Nike, and for pro cycling.

“Nimbl brings its expertise in materials, fit and customization, while Nike Cycling supports development with its expertise in innovation and design,” reads the note.

“The expanded partnership brings together the team’s elite racing insight with sport science and athlete-performance expertise from across Nike. It gives Team Visma-Lease a Bike, Nimbl, and Nike Cycling more opportunities to develop and test new ideas together under the conditions in which the riders compete,” it says.

The three-way collab will mark Nike’s biggest move in cycling in 15 years.

The humungous sportswear brand famously provided race kits for the U.S. Postal and then Radio Shack teams through the peak EPO era, and boasted a personal deal with Lance Armstrong.

Nike also sponsored the yellow, green, white, and polka dot jerseys of the Tour de France from 1996 through 2011.

However, the Portland powerhouse has kept its Swoosh outside the peloton since then, except for occasional shoe collabs.

Visma used special Nimbl x Nike cycling shoes during stages of both the Giro d’Italia and Tour de France in 2026, and Mark Cavendish often wore Nike-branded race kicks before he retired.

Nike also currently supplies Visma-Lease a Bike and women’s superteam FDJ United Suez with off-bike apparel, and has collaborated with Nimbl on two limited clothing ranges.

The expanded Nike deal comes at a key moment for Visma-Lease a Bike.

The Dutch team is hunting for a new backer, and its men’s division is struggling to keep pace with Tadej Pogačar and his UAE Emirates-XRG juggernaut.

Visma boss Richard Plugge suggested Wednesday that Nike could be crucial to the team’s future.

“We set a high standard for everything that helps us win, and that includes our kit. Nimbl is a specialist that shares that ambition. Bringing Nike Cycling’s expertise and creativity into the partnership opens up new possibilities for us,” Plugge said.

“Few brands have done as much as Nike to bring sport and athletes to a global audience. We’re proud to bring that experience into our partnership with Nike Cycling and take this next step together,” Plugge said.

“We want to build something together that moves both our team and the sport forward.”

There’s been speculation that Nike has been plotting a wider return to the pro peloton since it opened its apparel partnerships with Visma-Lease a Bike and FDJ United-Suez.

Speaking at the 2026 Tour de France, Nike project manager Kieran Ronan told WielerFlits that the brand isn’t ruling out a major return to bike racing.

With revenue of more than $50 billion a year, it would be one of the sport’s biggest brands.

However, Ronan said the consumer market comes first. Nike hasn’t made its own mass-market cycling kit since 2008.

“Everything is open for discussion at the moment,” Ronan said this summer. “The primary focus right now is on our return to this sport.

“We are closely monitoring professional cycling, but we are not losing sight of the needs of the recreational cyclist,” Ronan told Wielerflits . “We want to passionately provide them with the very best products. It is absolutely our ambition to play a major role in cycling again.”

Nike bulldozed into the world of trail and ultra running this year with its rebooted All Conditions Gear line and a swathe of high-profile team and race partnerships. Ten months later, Nike ACG is one of running’s hippest, most advanced clothing and trainer brands.

A play for the lucrative bike clothing market – a world where weekend warriors are willing to pay $200 for a jersey – might be next.

title: Riccardo Riccò Fires Back After Tadej Pogačar’s Ice Cream Quip About Doping
author: ahood
text:
Riccò, inset, reacted to some recent comments from Pogačar about 'selling ice cream.' (Photo: Gruber Images/Getty Images)

Tadej Pogačar didn’t name Riccardo Riccò outright in recent comments about doping in sport, but the banned-for-life ex-pro took it as a dig anyway.

Speaking to La Gazzetta dello Sport , Pogačar responded to a question about overnight anti-doping controls during this year’s Tour, when he and Jonas Vingegaard were among riders tested in the early hours before stage 15.

“Yes, you can be sure of it, doping does not exist now for the majority of the peloton,” Pogačar told La Gazzetta . “And besides, many want to stay in the environment even after the end of their careers, as sports directors, coaches … With one mistake, you risk ending up selling ice cream or something like that. No, the vast majority of the peloton would never do it.”

Pogačar didn’t name names, but Riccò — who runs ice cream shops in Italy — was quick to respond in an Instagram Story (now disappeared from his feed).

“I accept the dissing. It’s very funny. I’m up for the game. I actually expected it a lot sooner,” Riccò said in a video post in Italian, translated by Domestique .

“I have to say that it only takes a moment to end up making ice cream with me. So before talking, you’ve got to be 100 percent sure. I’ve seen a lot of people pass to the other side.”

Nicknamed the “Cobra,” Riccò has a lengthy doping rap sheet.

Riccò was riding for Saunier Duval when he tested positive for CERA at the 2008 Tour de France, after winning two stages. He was booted from the race, and the team pulled out. He later received a 12-year suspension after a 2011 blood transfusion, and Italy’s anti-doping tribunal banned him for life in 2020.

Mauro Gianetti, who managed Saunier Duval at the time and now leads UAE Emirates-XRG, told L’Équipe this summer that he had made mistakes in recruitment but denied responsibility for doping by his former riders.

Riccò, now 43, runs two gelato shops in Italy and organizes amateur cycling coaching and training camps.

Pogačar’s latest remarks were among his most candid on doping in the modern peloton.

“We race with heart and with the right mentality. We all know that prohibited, banned substances can damage your health. And, at the same time, cycling is a sport and nobody wants to risk their life for it,” he told La Gazzetta .

“Obviously, there will always be someone who tries to take a shortcut,” he said. “I have met so many riders over these years, and everyone loves cycling, the sport. Everyone dedicates 100 percent of their life to it; they commit to having proper nutrition, to preparing well. The coaches are good, there is a focus on recovery and we work tremendously hard.

“Nobody wants to risk losing all of this — it’s not worth it. We riders live for the sport in the right way and there is no desire to ruin ourselves.”

Pogačar is enjoying his final days of the off-season before joining his UAE teammates at a training camp in Spain.

title: AI may soon change what it means to be a theoretical physicist
author: Dan Kagan-Kans, Understanding AI
text:
About six months ago, Suvrat Raju, a professor of theoretical physics at the International Centre for Theoretical Sciences in Bengaluru, India, asked a frontier AI model to solve a physics problem. He didn’t ask because he needed to know the answer. He had actually solved this particular problem already. But he had never published the solution—which made it a perfect question to test how good AI was at physics.

LLMs have been trained on the whole Internet, so if a physics problem has been discussed online, it’s likely the model already knows about it and may have memorized the answer. So a fair test of AI capabilities needs to focus on problems that have never appeared online.

The model didn’t answer Raju’s problem correctly, but it did better than he expected—well, enough to get him thinking that the experiment should be repeated and formalized. With the help of a colleague, he set out to create a theoretical physics benchmark for AI.

title: Sri Lankan asylum seeker killed himself after being sent by UK to Eswatini
author: Rachel Savage in Johannesburg
text:
Kishanth Peramalya was denied entry due to sexual assault convictions and sent to Africa where he had no connections

The UK sent a Sri Lankan asylum seeker who had been convicted of sexual assault to Eswatini, a southern African country to which he had no connection and where he killed himself.

Kishanth Peramalya was part of a group that set sail from India hoping to reach Canada and claim asylum there. The boat was rescued by the Royal Navy in October 2021 when it got into difficulty and brought to Diego Garcia in the remote British Indian Ocean Territory, which hosts a US-UK military base.

In November 2024, the UK allowed 61 migrants to enter from Diego Garcia after a damning UN report about conditions in the camp. However, the then home secretary, Yvette Cooper, denied Peramalya entry to the UK due to his criminal convictions while he was on Diego Garcia for four counts of sexual assault, one count of assault occasioning actual bodily harm and one count of arson. Cooper’s decision was upheld by UK courts.

Peramalya had been granted protection from being returned to Sri Lanka, having been tortured and sexually abused by Sri Lankan military personnel as a teenager. In late March, the Maldives said it would take him for 30 days, according to the BBC . He was then transferred to Eswatini, a country landlocked by South Africa and Mozambique and formerly known as Swaziland, where he killed himself on 13 September.

A draft deal between the UK and Eswatini governments would have committed Downing Street to cover the costs of Peramalya’s resettlement there for three years, according to the BBC, which said the UK was also finalising arrangements for Peramalya to live in Eswatini permanently.

The Guardian has not seen the draft deal. Thabile Mdluli, a spokesperson for Eswatini’s government, said: “The initial arrangement was temporary in nature and intended to safeguard Mr Peramalya’s safety while the government of the United Kingdom worked towards a long-term solution regarding his circumstances.”

She said that no formal agreement was ever reached over Peramalya’s long-term residency status with the UK and declined to comment further on the specific arrangements of his stay in Eswatini or the circumstances around his death.

Mdluli said: “Eswatini has not received any other similar request from the government of the United Kingdom. The government of the Kingdom of Eswatini remains committed to ensuring that any agreements entered into with external partners safeguard national interest as well as the safety and security of Emaswati [Swazi people].”

A UK government spokesperson said: “Keeping the British public safe will always be our first priority, and we will continue to take the decisions necessary to protect the British people. That includes taking steps to ensure high harm foreign criminals cannot enter the UK. We continue to work with the Eswatini authorities in relation to this case.”

Peramalya had post-traumatic stress disorder and attempted suicide multiple times on Diego Garcia, according to a UK high court judgment in February 2025.

Peramalya’s family told the BBC he was initially housed alone in an isolated guesthouse in Eswatini. “My brother did not want to go there at all,” said his sister, speaking from India. “He couldn’t manage being there alone, he was very lonely.”

She said he had called her four times a day and was initially having weekly psychiatric appointments, which were made daily when his mental health deteriorated, as well as having someone brought in to prepare his food.

Peramalya’s relatives said they were not aware of his convictions for sexual offences or any plan to make his transfer to Eswatini permanent.

Eswatini has accepted dozens of third-country deportees from the US since July 2025. In November 2025, its government confirmed it had received $5.1m in exchange for taking up to 160 migrants from the US.

title: Indian Cockroach movement leader asks court for permission to fly to UK
author: Amrit Dhillon in Delhi
text:
Officials at Delhi airport stopped Saurav Das from boarding flight to Britain, where students have invited him to speak

A leader of India’s youth-led Cockroach movement has asked the Delhi high court to give him permission to fly to the UK after immigration officials at Delhi airport stopped him boarding a flight early on Tuesday morning.

The court is scheduled to hear Saurav Das’s case on Thursday morning. His lawyer asked the court for a quick hearing because Das has by now already missed some of his engagements at British universities and can only attend the other events on his itinerary if he is allowed to fly out as soon as possible.

Das, 27, is one of the main faces of the Cockroach movement, which shot into the political firmament out of nowhere in May to challenge the Narendra Modi government with street protests.

The movement succeeded in forcing the education minister to resign in July over exam leaks and has since functioned as a pressure group.

Das had been invited by the Oxford Union Society to participate in a “fireside chat” on the movement.

Indian student groups at Edinburgh, Cambridge, Queen Mary University of London and the London School of Economics have also invited him to speak.

“Students want to know how we succeeded without any violence, how we began and where we are going. There is a great curiosity about the movement,” Das told the Guardian.

Reports in the Indian media have alleged that Das was informed well before the flight that his passport contained discrepancies.

“None of these reports is true,” said Das. “I received an email five hours before my flight saying that I should not use my passport for travel. It gave no reason. And I did not see the email until I arrived at Delhi airport. What’s more, I’ve travelled abroad before on this passport since it was issued in 2019 so what’s the problem with it now?”

He suspects that the government is using a frivolous case filed in Chennai against him as a pretext. The case has been filed, Das surmises, by someone hostile to the Cockroach movement and disputes his citizenship.

Das believes he was deliberately stopped by a government that is “scared” of someone such as him speaking abroad about the ideals of Mahatma Gandhi and Jawaharlal Nehru (independent India’s first prime minister) and that it wanted to make an example of him.

“It’s a chilling signal to young Indians that we can do what we like, that if we can do this to a leader of a movement, we can do this to you too,” said Das.

In recent years, the government has stopped foreign speakers and academics, including several from the UK, from entering India.

Last year, Francesca Orsini, a professor at Soas University of London, was stopped at Delhi airport and deported despite holding a valid visa. The government said she had been blacklisted for allegedly conducting research and speaking at events while visiting on a tourist visa in 2024.

Also last year, Nitasha Kaul, a professor at Westminster University, was detained at Bangalore airport and deported for “anti-India activities”.

Some people who find themselves blacklisted have chosen to fight back. In 2023, the UK-based journalist Amrit Wilson had her overseas citizen of India card which allows free movement into India cancelled, also for alleged “anti-India activities”.

She took legal action and earlier this week, the Delhi high court ruled that the government had failed to give any concrete details of what it meant by “anti-India activities”.

The court has given the government a week to issue a fresh notice, this time giving specific reasons.

title: Alonso: “We can't be competitive with the power unit we have”
These Are the Biggest Changes Coming to Pro Cycling in 2027
author: Jim Cotton
text:
Big changes are coming to pro cycling in 2027, and we aren’t talking about Tadej Pogačar not wearing a rainbow jersey.

Tour de France hopefuls are making daring transfers.

Long-time backers are switching allegiances.

Races will be in different places, teams will have unwieldy new names, and the UCI will have implemented more rules when competition restarts in January.

A lot has changed in the world of pro cycling in the past few months – some things more important than others.

We’re not going to list every tiny tweak that’s been made to the pro peloton this off-season. Nobody wants to read that, not even us nerds at Velo HQ.

Instead, here are the changes for 2027 that you really need to know about – the ones being debated at every group ride and that will drive the narrative into the future.

Last year’s transfer window was wild. Remco Evenepoel and Demi Vollering both made moves that transformed their new teams’ futures.

There have been some similarly seismic transfers this winter – particularly in the women’s peloton.

Kasia Niewiadoma-Phinney and Paula Blasi – two of the few women who might dethrone Queen Demi – both made blockbuster moves in the quest for the yellow jersey.

Meanwhile, Cecilie Uttrup Ludwig is looking for a career reboot with her “home” team, Uno-X Mobility, and the wildly underrated Cédrine Kebaol is jumping on the SD Worx-Protime juggernaut.

Niewiadoma’s move to Lidl-Trek will thrust the women’s team from relative anonymity into Tour de France contention. Blasi’s decision to team up with Marlen Reusser will elevate Movistar to a superteam on-par with FDJ and SD Worx.

Expect a shift in the Women’s WorldTour hierarchy next year.

The shakeup on the men’s side has been similarly huge, albeit maybe less transformational.

First up – no, Paul Seixas is not leaving Decathlon CMA CGM, yet .

Instead, NSN Cycling Team took the spotlight by landing the two biggest male transfers of the winter – Primoz Roglič and Richard Carapaz.

These ageless wonders won’t be worrying Pogačar in 2027, but they could bring NSN grand tour top-fives, countless stage wins, and endless entertainment.

A team that scrapped for stage wins with little success in 2026 will be a factor in 2027.

The success of Roglič’s season could also dictate how long he sticks in pro cycling. Will 2027 be Rogla’s last dance?

Felix Gall’s move to Lidl-Trek will be equally intriguing. Can the Austrian jump from the lower steps of stage-race podiums with a Lidl-Trek team that’s already bloated with wannabe grand tour winners?

If you’re still calling Jim Ratcliffe’s team “Ineos Grenadiers” and thought Michael Matthews rides for “Mitchelton Scott,” we’ve got bad news.

A slew of new team names is coming to pro cycling in 2027.

Quick-Step is out. After 24 years of cobbles and swagger, the very-Belgian flooring brand is done with bikes.

Instead, The Wolfpack will become Soudal-Safety Jogger in 2027 after the burly boot ‘n’ workwear brand stepped up as co-title partner.

Now that’s a name that’ll take some getting used to.

That said, it’s a refreshing blue-collar throwback to when the peloton was powered by everyday superstores, obscure farming equipment , and carpet brands.

On the flipside, brace for a bunch more obscure tech, finance, and IT companies placing their names inside pro cycling in 2027.

Canyon-SRAM is diving into investment and trading in partnership with Scalable Capital after its recent experiment with the Zondacrypto exchange ended in disaster .

Meanwhile, the team once known as TotalEnergies has been rescued by title sponsorship from Xefi, one of those IT brands that does business things you don’t really understand.

On that note – watch out who you call TotalEnergies in 2027.

TotalEnergies has totally withdrawn from the men’s peloton ahead of 2027 so it can go all-in on a long-term deal with the newly named TotalEnergies-FDJ United. As a reminder, the oil giant also terminated its non-naming deal with Netcompany Ineos .

In the long-term, TotalEnergies’ pivot could mark a tipping point for women’s cycling – it will be one of the biggest backers in the Women’s WorldTour and is committed for five years.

In the short term, it contributes another confusing team name to remember.

Sorry Bianchi fans, there won’t be any celeste in the pro peloton in 2027.

Bianchi’s problems extended from its year-end accounts to its stake in professional sport this autumn when Bahrain-Victorious dropped the historic Italian brand in favor of Factor.

As an aside while chatting cult brands with financial fears – Rapha is coming back to bike racing with Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe.

The other headline in terms of bike sponsorship?

The Shandong-based manufacturer Pardus will join XDS in the premier cycling calendar in a blockbuster three-year deal with Xefi (that’s the team that was TotalEnergies, remember).

Pardus’ entry into elite cycling continues a paradigm shift in team-bike partnership.

The Chinese giant XDS blazed a trail by partnering with Astana in 2025 and then Laboral Kutxa-Fundación Euskada in 2026. Guangdong brand Quick-Pro followed suit with Euskaltel Euskadi in 2026.

Pardus is the next Chinese manufacturer looking to disrupt the Western-centric lockdown on pro cycling.

Heritage brands like Bianchi should take note – China is coming, fast.

One established Western manufacturer that needn’t be worried?

Yes, the behemoth U.S. manufacturer has split from the Quick-Step franchise after 18 years , but that’s because it’s so busy with three superteams from different corners of the sport: Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe, TotalEnergies-FDJ United, and Specialized Off-Road.

The men’s and women’s Vueltas are on the move, USA loses out, and the world championships will be premature in the 2027 race calendar.

USA loses one of its marquee UCI-rated races. The Maryland Cycling Classic is shuttering for good.…

title: ‘We Were in Over Our Heads’: Inside the Wild Debut of America’s New Pro Cycling Team
author: ahood
text:
Oliver's big wins were the highlight of Modern Adventure's inaugural season. (Photo: DAVID PINTENS / Belga / AFP via Getty Images)

Modern Adventure Pro Cycling bet on a bunch of overlooked and undervalued riders in its first season, and came away with five wins and a world title on the track.

That’s according to coach Bobby Julich , who told Velo’s Hannah Gross at El Tour de Tucson that the inaugural season for America’s new cycling team delivered some sweet highs and a few gut punches .

Nothing was certain in the first major American men’s pro team in decades , but race organizers noticed how the riders stuck together on the roughest days.

“Everywhere George and I went, it was compliments of, ‘hey, you guys not only just showed up but you represented,’” Julich told Velo . “Yes, we were in over our heads quite a bit, but the guys rode together as a team. They fought together as a team, they enjoyed each other’s company, and we’re only going to get better from here.”

Julich said that sense of collective mission carried the team across 2026.

There’s a feeling of mission accomplished from season one .

Coming into the team’s winter camps, Julich said the momentum is already building for what everyone expects to be an even bigger 2027.

At the beginning of the year, co-founder George Hincapie described his team as a bit like the “Bad News Bears” of cycling.

The sport directors and staff stitched together a 21-rider roster this year based on riders who Julich said “fell through the cracks.”

“They’ve been told that they’re not good enough or they’re never going to make it, and then they come to our team,” Julich told Velo . “We supported them and gave them the confidence that it takes and the support that it needs. And they just blossomed.”

That sense of being underdogs and something to prove drove them across their first season.

Julich recounted a key moment early in the year when Mark Stewart, a journeyman from Scotland, expressed what it meant to the riders to be a part of the team.

“And he looked around the room, and he looked at me straight in the eye, and he said, ‘What you see here is seven of the most supported, confident, and happy people that we’ve ever been,’” Julich said. “That set the tone, that set the standard, and from there, even in races where we got slapped around pretty good, those guys stuck together.”

The results came. Stefan de Bod finished fourth overall at the AlUla Tour in the team’s first race, just 25 seconds off the win.

Five of its seven starters made it to the velodrome at Paris-Roubaix, including 23-year-old Cole Kessler.

Ben Oliver, a former mountain biker who finally earned a real wage racing bikes, won two stages and the overall at the Ethias Tour de Wallonie, a 2.Pro stage race in Belgium that gave the team its biggest success of the year.

Riley Pickrell delivered one more win to close out the road season at the Tour de Langkawi.

By October, Stewart won the points race at the UCI track worlds in Shanghai.

“For us as a first-year organization to have one of our riders win a world championship in any discipline is massive,” Julich said.

For season two, the team is upping its ambitions.

The team will race as Modern Adventure Factor Racing, with the bike brand stepping up as co-title sponsor to help the team’s goal of reaching the Tour de France within five years.

Modern Adventure brings on four new riders for 2027, and since everyone was signed to two-year deals, the roster jumps from 21 riders to 25 .

Modern Adventure adds WorldTour veteran Jonas Rutsch, sixth at Paris-Roubaix in 2025, from Lotto Intermarché, and reigning Australian road champion and WorldTour giant-killer Patrick Eddy from Team Brennan.

The team also signs New Zealand climber Josh Burnett from Burgos Burpellet BH, and Owen Cole, the 2023 U.S. U23 road champion and 2026 Tour de la Guadeloupe winner, from Team Winston Salem-Flow.

“We don’t yet have the pressure of getting UCI points or to get in the WorldTour,” Julich told Velo . “That’s a year or two further down the road that we have to start worrying about that.”

For 2027, it’s all about building on its first season and targeting even better results.

The team has yet to pin down its racing calendar, but it’s already confirmed for the Tour Colombia, which run January 26-31. The team is hoping to broaden its spring classics campaign to get into some of the hillier Ardennes-style one-days.

A grand tour is still a dream, but the team must hit the top-30 in the world team rankings before it qualifies. Modern Adventure ended 2026 ranked 36th, so inching up the rankings will start to matter going into 2028 if the teams wants a grand tour bid.

“What I learned the most is that when you get good people, passionate people, working together, regardless of their experience, that you’re going to have fun and be successful,” Julich said. “What we want to do in the future is just build upon what we did this year.”

title: Are Manchester United this season's Tottenham?
text:
Last season, Tottenham - a member of the so-called 'big six' - escaped relegation from the Premier League on the final day.

Now, with Manchester United making their worst start to a league season since 1972, it begs the question: are United this season's Spurs?

Well while Tottenham finished 17th with just 41 points, they actually started the season better than United have. After 11 games last season, Spurs were riding high in fifth with 18 points - 10 more than United have now.

But one of the biggest myths in football is 'the table never lies' and it was certainly lying about Tottenham at this stage last season.

While the table was prompting talk of a possible Champions League place, expected goals (xG) had already recognised a relegation battle lay ahead for Tottenham, even predicting the position they'd finish in.

United's expected goal difference is almost identical to Tottenham's at this stage last season, but this time the table is more honest, even if United are perhaps not as bad as it makes out.

But there's no denying United's statistics are those of a team in a relegation battle, with many of them in the bottom six of Premier League teams this season.

While United have performed poorly defensively, their attack is actually not bad.

Remarkably, United have taken the most shots in the Premier League so far this season, and their expected goals scored figure is in the top five.

But what new head coach Mauricio Pochettino has to implement quickly is some quality control when it comes to shots at both ends of the pitch. United are converting just 7% of their chances and conceding 16% of their opponents' - a poor combination for any team.

And it's not simply down to finishing or shot-stopping, though they should have scored a few more. Based on xG per shot, United are currently taking the second-worst chances to score and giving up the easiest ones at the back.

As a result, Opta give United just over a one-in-four chance of being relegated at the end of the season (27.5%), making them the fifth-most likely side to go down after Crystal Palace, Sunderland, Ipswich and Coventry.

By analysing historical and team performances as well as the strength of opponents, Opta predict the % chance of each club finishing in each position in the League.

While the above means it's more likely United will survive, it's worth noting the one position Opta predicts United are most likely to finish is 18th, with a 10.1% chance. That would mean the 13-time Premier League winners are relegated.

There's a 90% chance they finish anywhere else, but the next most likely are the three places just above the relegation zone, including a 9.9% chance of them finishing where Tottenham did last season.

History also suggests a relegation battle lies ahead for United given their poor start.

Of the 26 previous sides that had exactly eight points after 11 games, 13 survived and 13 were relegated. Among those that stayed up, only four finished more than six points above the danger zone.

A top-half finish looks unlikely. Since the competition became a 20-team league in 1995-96, no side has ever finished in the top half after taking eight points or fewer from their first 11 games.

Two teams did finish there more than 30 years ago but they had four more games to climb the table as teams played 42 games a season in those days.

Having said that, both were in the top half at the 38-game mark so United finishing there wouldn't be entirely unprecedented.

It's a big ask, though, as the club have already taken 19 points fewer from the fixtures they've played than they did last season.

Even if they were to repeat the results that led to them finishing third from now on, they would still only reach 52 points, the number Chelsea narrowly finished 10th with last season

Though United are without a win in nine Premier League matches, their remaining fixtures of 2026 do offer some hope.

While they have a tough home game against Brentford this weekend and a trip to champions Arsenal just before Christmas, their other five games are against teams currently in the bottom seven - sides we must, at this point, call relegation rivals

So despite suffering the worst first game by a Manchester United manager for 100 years in the 4-0 defeat at Liverpool , Pochettino will hope to quickly quash any concerns his new club will be embroiled in the same fight as his former one last season.

title: Why tiny cars are taking off across Europe
text:
Selena Buse, 16, reverses her Citroën Ami out of a parking space and heads off past the school playground. Heads turn. The Ami looks pretty remarkable. Futurist or like-a-toaster depending on your point of view. But it's changed her life.

"I got it because I really needed it to get to school. And I use it to visit friends on the weekends. It's indispensable in rural areas like where I live," she says.

In France, you can drive a car like this from the age of 14 with a road safety certificate and eight hours training. In Italy too.

In Germany and Spain it's 15, in the UK 16. Because they are classed as motorised quadri-cycles. Four-wheel mopeds in other words.

Registrations have risen from about 13,000 in 2019 to around 25,000 last year in France.

In Europe, sales have gone from 30,000 to 60,000 in the past five years. And the Ami, launched in 2020, has really changed the image, with teenagers who now account for a quarter of all mini-car sales.

In Selena's very small Citroën, we are soon rolling along at the top speed of 45km/h (28mph). For other road users, no-licence cars like this can seem like mobile traffic calming.

"When I'm on faster roads and there's a lot of traffic the cars behind me sometimes honk their horns but I can't go any quicker!" Selena says.

Another local Daniel Laprès, who drives a micro-car made by French firm and market-leader Aixam, tells me he actually pulls over to let the cars behind pass.

He and his wife moved from Paris to this country village two years ago. Of Canadian nationality, he didn't swap his foreign licence for a French one in time and lost the right to drive. That didn't matter much when he was in Paris. Like many Parisians he didn't need a car. He used public transport. But that's not possible here.

"We tried living off of taxis and it was in the end a disaster. Then we heard about how you could drive without having to have a licence, and it was the exact solution to our problem. Cheap, inexpensive to operate, basically no administrative formalities, you get insurance."

However, Laprès feels less safe in his small car. "They're little more than tin cans on wheels, right? I mean, you're not going to be driving fast, but someone else could be."

These cars are forbidden on motorways. But even on medium-fast roads, being considerably slower than the average vehicle can be a problem.

"You go on national highways at your risk and peril. I did it once and I will never, ever do it again. On those roads (speed limit 110km/h), everybody is passing you, including the biggest trucks. And they come at you very fast from the rear, so it's scary," Laprès says.

Daniel is 77 so fits in with the long-established market for these cars: older people living in the countryside.

Traditionally the market also included quite a few people who'd lost their licences, often because of drink-driving offenses. But the launch of the electric Citroën Ami in 2020 changed the customer profile and the product.

"The launch of the Ami was the beginning of the transformation of the sector, with more and more electric models coming on to the market. In 2026, more than 67% of new licence-free cars are electric," says Marie-Laure Nivot, market analyst at AAA Data.

This tendency was encouraged by stricter EU regulations on motorised two-wheelers that had been the vehicles of choice for European teenagers until then.

"It proved too costly for manufacturers to apply the new EU rules, so mopeds and small scooters have almost disappeared from the market since 2020 and licence-free cars have taken their place," Marie-Laure Nivot says.

Tiny car sales rose strongly till 2024 although they have flattened since in France with the withdrawal of subsidies for electric models.

Curiously, the arrival in this niche market of a giant competitor in the shape of Stellantis brand Citroën was actually good news for existing French manufacturers like Aixam and Ligier.

"We're specialised in this niche market and we're very good at what we do, but of course, we didn't have the communication strength of a multinational like Stellantis. They helped us to make people understand that it was possible in France to drive this product from 14-years-old, in Germany from 15-years-old. They gave a lot of visibility to our market," says Aixam sales and marketing director Tom Faget.

Aixam has invested €30m (£25m; $33m) in expanding its production capacity in France. And its sales are growing in other European countries, even as the French market slows.

Meanwhile, the competition is producing increasingly sophisticated minicars - some costing as much as a small conventional car. At Ligier, marketing director Romain Illegems says the biggest change is in who's buying them.

"We've gone from mobility that was imposed on people to mobility that people choose. Before, these vehicles were something you used because you absolutely needed to get around, because there was no public transport, or because you didn't have a licence.

"Today, teenagers are choosing them instead of scooters or mopeds, because they're safer and offer better protection from the weather. Young people now account for 40% of our customers."

There are limitations, of course. Just two seats, a maximum speed of 45km/h and no motorways. But for Selena, who rents her Ami for €60 a month, plus insurance, it's a small price to pay for independence.
